title: NAT in depth
summary: SNAT, DNAT, PAT and 1:1 NAT, the NAT table, hairpinning, and carrier-grade NAT.

steps.title: The NAT vocabulary
body: | **SNAT** | source address of outgoing packets | office -> internet |
| **PAT / NAPT / masquerade** | source address **and port**, many inside hosts share one IP | every home router |
| **DNAT / port forwarding** | destination of incoming packets | public :443 -> 10.0.0.5:443 |
| **1:1 static NAT** | one public IP maps to one inside host, all ports | cloud "elastic IP" |
The router keeps a **NAT table** (conntrack) keyed by the connection:
Two inside hosts can use the same source port; PAT gives them different public ports.

steps.prompt: Match each scenario to the kind of NAT.
pairs: 30 laptops browse through one public IP
Public port 8443 reaches an internal web server
A cloud VM has its own public IP mapped to its private one
Office traffic leaves with a fixed public address

steps.prompt: How many simultaneous connections can share one public IP to the **same** remote endpoint, using ports 1024-65535? Per user with 64 users?
steps.explain: Both ends count, hence the `+ 1`. Port exhaustion is real behind busy NATs, which is why CGNAT assigns port blocks and cloud NAT gateways add IPs.

steps.title: Why NAT breaks inbound
body: A NAT entry is created only by an **outgoing** packet. An unsolicited packet arriving at the public IP matches nothing and is dropped.
That's why peer-to-peer apps, game hosts and VoIP need port forwards, UPnP, or tricks like **hole punching** (both sides send out first, via a rendezvous server) and relays (TURN).
**Hairpinning (NAT loopback):** an inside client connects to the router's **public** IP to reach a port-forwarded server that's also inside.

Without hairpin NAT, the server replies directly to the client's private address, the client doesn't recognise the reply, and it fails. Fix with hairpin NAT or **split DNS** (inside clients resolve the name to the private IP).

**CGNAT:** ISPs short of IPv4 put customers behind *their own* NAT, using `100.64.0.0/10`. Your router's WAN address is then not public: port forwards on your router can't work, and many customers share one public IP (so one abuser can get it blocked for all).

steps.prompt: Will an unsolicited inbound connection reach the inside host?
items: Port forward configured on a router with a public WAN IP
1:1 NAT with a firewall rule allowing it
Port forward on a router whose WAN IP is 100.64.12.7
Reply to a connection the inside host opened

steps.prompt: `nas.home.example` resolves to your public IP and works from your phone on 4G, but not from your laptop at home. Most likely?
options: No hairpin NAT on the router; use NAT loopback or make the name resolve to the NAS's private IP inside
steps.explain: From outside, DNAT works. From inside, the reply takes a shortcut and breaks.

steps.prompt: You set up a port forward but nothing from the internet arrives. The router's WAN shows `100.72.4.19`. Why?
options: You're behind carrier-grade NAT; the ISP's NAT drops it before your router. Ask for a public IP, use IPv6, or a tunnel
100.72.x is your public IP, check the firewall
steps.explain: 100.64.0.0/10 is shared address space for CGNAT.

steps.title: Classify a WAN address
prompt: Write `string Wan(string ip)` describing a router's WAN address: `"CGNAT"` for 100.64.0.0/10, `"private (double NAT)"` for the RFC 1918 ranges,
starter: uint ToUInt(string ip) => ip.Split('.').Aggregate(0u, (acc, o) => (acc << 8) | uint.Parse(o));
uint MaskOf(int prefix) => prefix == 0 ? 0u : uint.MaxValue << (32 - prefix);
solution: uint ToUInt(string ip) => ip.Split('.').Aggregate(0u, (acc, o) => (acc << 8) | uint.Parse(o));
uint MaskOf(int prefix) => prefix == 0 ? 0u : uint.MaxValue << (32 - prefix);
bool In(string net, int p) => (a & MaskOf(p)) == ToUInt(net);
hints: A local function `In(net, prefix)` keeps it short.

steps.title: A PAT table
prompt: - `string Outbound(string inside, string remote)` returns `"{publicIp}:{port}"` for this inside endpoint talking to this remote endpoint.
The same pair reuses its port; a new pair gets the next port from 40000 upward.
- `string? Inbound(string remote, int port)` returns the inside endpoint only if a mapping exists on that port **and** the packet comes from the remote it was created for, else `null`.
- `int Count` is the number of mappings.
solution: private readonly Dictionary<string, int> outMap = new();
private readonly Dictionary<int, (string Inside, string Remote)> inMap = new();
public string Outbound(string inside, string remote)
public string? Inbound(string remote, int port)
=> inMap.TryGetValue(port, out var e) && e.Remote == remote ? e.Inside : null;
template: Dojo.Eq("stranger on a mapped port", null, dojoT.Inbound("6.6.6.6:443", 40000));
hints: Inbound needs both the port and the remote to match.
